introduction.p: A graph sketch combines the domain, intercepts, limits, derivative signs, extrema, and concavity. We will organize this information to draw a graph consistent with the function's formulas and limiting behavior.

exercise.title: Why do we need both f' and f'' to sketch a graph?

statement.p: The first derivative gives direction; the second gives bending. In your own words, why is a sign chart for f' not enough by itself, and what extra truth does a sign chart for f'' add to a sketch?

hint.p: Two graphs can both rise and still look different: one can bend like a cup, the other like a cap. Local extrema and inflection points come from different sign changes.

subsection.title: Asymptotes and end behavior
subsection.p: Polynomials do not have vertical asymptotes. Rational functions often do.
Derivative information describes shape where the function exists. Limits describe what happens near missing points and far away.

exercise.title: Why do limits, not derivatives, describe asymptotes?

statement.p: Derivatives describe shape where the function exists. Vertical, horizontal, and slant asymptotes are statements about missing points and about far-away behavior. In your own words, why must a complete sketch ask what happens as x approaches a break and as x\to\pm\infty?

hint.p: A derivative cannot see a hole or an infinite jump that sits outside the domain. Those features are limits.

subsection.title: A complete curve-sketching workflow
subsection.p: A calculus sketch should gather evidence in an organized way.

The workflow is not a rigid machine. Sometimes symmetry saves work. Sometimes a limit matters more than a derivative. Sometimes a derivative is too complicated to factor nicely. But the questions are steady.

exercise.title: Why is a calculus sketch a summary of evidence rather than a guess?

statement.p: The curve-sketching workflow gathers domain, intercepts, asymptotes, first-derivative signs, and second-derivative signs before any picture is drawn. In your own words, why should the sketch obey that evidence, and why is a pretty picture that violates one of those facts not yet a calculus sketch?

hint.p: The goal is not a perfect drawing. The goal is a picture that tells the truth about rising, falling, bending, and end behavior.

subsection.title: When technology helps and when it misleads
subsection.p: A graphing calculator or computer can help check a sketch, but it should not replace the analysis.
Technology draws what it samples. It can miss a hole, hide an asymptote, or make a bad viewing window look convincing.

paragraphs.title: A misleading window
paragraphs.p: has vertical asymptotes at x=-1 and x=1. But if we only graph it on the window
we see only the middle branch. The graph may look like a small decreasing curve with a flat point at the origin. That window hides the asymptotes and the outer branches.
A graphing device answers the question we ask it. Calculus helps us ask better questions:
A good sketch uses both tools: computation for speed, and calculus for judgment.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: Graph sketching often leads back to limits. A vertical asymptote is a limit. A horizontal or slant asymptote is a limit. End behavior is a limit.
Some limits are easy. Others have a strange form. For example,
has numerator and denominator both approaching 0. The quotient could approach a number, blow up, or fail to settle.
The next section gives a derivative-based tool for such limits. Once again, local linear approximation will explain the rule.
